abstract: Abstract The SysteMHC Atlas v1.0 was the first public repository dedicated to mass spectrometry-based immunopeptidomics. Here we introduce a newly released version of the SysteMHC Atlas v2.0 ( https://systemhc.sjtu.edu.cn ), a comprehensive collection of 7190 MS files from 303 allotypes. We extended and optimized a computational pipeline that allows the identification of MHC-bound peptides carrying on unexpected post-translational modifications (PTMs), thereby resulting in 471K modified peptides identified over 60 distinct PTM types. In total, we identified approximately 1.0 million and 1.1 million unique peptides for MHC class I and class II immunopeptidomes, respectively, indicating a 6.8-fold increase and a 28-fold increase to those in v1.0. The SysteMHC Atlas v2.0 introduces several new features, including the inclusion of non-UniProt peptides, and the incorporation of several novel computational tools for FDR estimation, binding affinity prediction and motif deconvolution. Additionally, we enhanced the user interface, upgraded website framework, and provided external links to other resources related. Finally, we built and provided various spectral libraries as community resources for data mining and future immunopeptidomic and proteomic analysis. We believe that the SysteMHC Atlas v2.0 is a unique resource to provide key insights to the immunology and proteomics community and will accelerate the development of vaccines and immunotherapies.

Introduction
Activating the immune system to fight disease, cancer immunotherapy has become an essential part of treatment for diverse cancers (
1–3
). Major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules (human leukocyte antigen [HLA] molecules in humans) present short peptides on the cell surface for the recognition by T cells, which is in the center of immunotherapy (
4–6
). Being highly polymorphic, the MHC of each individual can bind a unique set of short peptides. Comprehensive characterization of the entirety of such MHC-bound peptides, collectively referred to as the MHC immunopeptidome, is essential to advance our understanding of immunology and provide the foundation to design vaccines effectively and safely (
7–9
).
Mass spectrometry (MS) is the state-of-the-art method to study the immunopeptidome, which enables the identification of thousands of MHC-bound peptides in one single MS measurement (
9
,
10
). MS-based immunopeptidomics provides direct experimental evidence of MHC-bound peptides and has been successfully applied to the analysis of various sample types (
11
,
12
), such as tumor and healthy tissues (
13–17
), as well as plasma samples (
18–20
).
In the year of 2017, we launched the SysteMHC atlas project, a first-of-its-kind data repository that aims at collecting, organizing and sharing immunopeptidomic data generated by MS (
21
,
22
). Accelerated by Nobel prize winners James P. Allison and Tasuku Honjo for their findings on cancer immunotherapy, the field of immunopepdomics kept growing at a rapid speed over the last six years, resulting in the continuous accumulation of huge amounts of MS-based immunopeptidomic datasets. It is especially true for MHC class II immunopeptidome (
23
,
24
). At the same time, the analytical power of MS instruments, computational tools for binding affinity prediction and motif deconvolution all got developed and improved, as experimentally validated shreds of evidence that are needed to build computational models accumulated (
24–26
).
Altering protein structure, properties and interactions, post-translational modifications (PTMs) are critical molecular mechanisms that regulate protein functions and have the potential to vastly expand the repository of the immunopeptidome. Previously, the SysteMHC Atlas only identified modified peptides containing oxidized methionine which is normally included as an experimentally derived artificial modification in proteomics workflows, because it was technically challenging to consider multiple possible PTM types due to their ever-expanded search space. Recent development and maturation of computational approaches support the identification of MHC-bound peptides carrying on unexpected PTMs. Applying similar strategies, several labs (
11–13
) have independently reported the occurrence of various PTM types found on the immunopeptidome and revealed the impacts that might have on the presentation of cancer antigens to T cells (
27–29
). Therefore, there is a great demand to update the SysteMHC Atlas with more resources and to re-analyze the whole data repository with improved tools.
To date, several databases have been built to collect MS-based HLA peptides, such as HLA Ligand Atlas (
13
) and caAtlas (
28
). By analyzing or collecting MS measurements of ∼1000 human samples, both databases have provided lists of HLA-bound peptides as valuable resources for immunopeptidomic studies. However, apart from identifications of peptides, none of the MS data can be further utilized or mined in these databases, which presents a missing opportunity in expanding the pool of immunopeptidome. Indeed, once properly organized, MS data can be stored as spectral libraries that ensure easy usage and enjoy greater sensitivity for question-driven proteomic analysis. Moreover, the species in these databases is only restricted to human, and the MS measurements generated or collected were dominantly generated in one or several labs. Until now, no other specialized database, to our knowledge, has been devoted to collecting, storing, analyzing, and more importantly, disseminating MS-based immunopeptidomic data that were generated at significant expense for data mining or future usage.
To meet these critical demands, we have updated the SysteMHC Atlas to version 2.0 (Figure
1A
) with an extensive collection of over 7000 MS measurements and the incorporation of a few novel computational tools (Table
1
). With all these features, the SysteMHC Atlas (v2.0) can serve as a more useful community resource to provide key insights to the immunology and proteomics community, and will accelerate the development of vaccines and immunotherapies against various immune-related diseases.

Building and benchmarking an updated computational pipeline
Compared with the original pipeline built in v1.0, the new computational pipeline (Figure
1B
) includes four major updates: (i) identification of MHC-bound peptides carrying on unexpected PTMs; (ii) accurate FDR estimation by three different methods. This is important because FDR estimation is usually challenging for MHC identification due to its huge search space. The three methods applied are: Global FDR estimation (by default); separated FDR estimation (unmodified versus modified) and Transferred FDR estimation (
34
). Specifically, the transferred FDR estimation method is useful for rare modifications that often result in a very small number of modified peptide identifications, which makes the other two FDR estimation methods inaccurate due to the inadequate sample size; (iii) incorporation of novel computational tools for binding affinity prediction and motif deconvolution (
26
,
36–38
). Indeed, multiple sophisticated computational tools have recently been developed and were included in the pipeline. Those tools can run in parallel to provide information that may be complementary to each other. In this way, users have the option to investigate the results generated from various algorithms via a user-friendly web portal; (iv) identification of peptides not found in UniProt, but identified using protein databases that were customized by the authors of the original study. Those peptides are referred as ‘non-UniProt peptides’ and may represent a wide array of both canonical and non-canonical peptides. For instance, non-UniProt canonical peptides may represent tumor-specific mutated peptides, whereas non-UniProt non-canonical peptides may represent tumor-specific non-mutated peptides from non-coding regions of the genomes, or from other non-canonical genomic sources, as described (
39
). Note that an exhaustive classification of those non-UniProt peptides will be made available in a future version of the atlas.
We benchmarked our new computational pipeline using a public immunopeptidomic dataset (
40
). Compared with the original results of identifications (
40
), we found a 50–150% improved sensitivity in terms of the number of peptides and binders identified (
Supplementary Figure S1
). The gained set of peptides that were uniquely identified by our workflow showed a similar binding motif to that of shared peptides identified by both pipelines, indicating a high degree of reliability of peptides and binders identified by our computational workflow.
To enable reproducible and transparent bioinformatics analysis, the whole pipeline was built based on nextflow, allowing one-stop immunopeptidomic data analysis (
41
). For local use of the pipeline, we provided Docker images, to ensure easy use and being compatible with all operating systems including Windows, Linux and MacOS. The pipeline offers various options such as number of threads, memory size, search mode, protein database, etc. By default, it generates the tables of identified peptides and MHC-bound peptides with various scores for identification and binding affinity prediction by different tools, the plots of allele-specific binding motif analyzed by MoDec-v1.2 and GibbsGluster-v2.0 (
37
,
38
), and the spectral libraries associated. We believe that the computational pipeline facilitates the processing and interpretation of immunopeptidomic datasets and will further enhance the impact of the atlas.
The atlas
In July 2023, our atlas contained 184.8 million tandem mass spectra obtained from 7190 mass spectrometric raw files collected mainly from PRIDE (
42
), MASSIVE, iProX (
43
) and jPOST (
44
). Based on the information available on the publications, we further curated them by, (i) associating each file with biological samples and completing the metadata including tissue type, cell type, disease type, MS instrument and fragmentation method; (ii) classifying them into MHC class I and class II samples and (iii) assigning the allotypes, if available, to each sample. In terms of both technical aspects (such as MS instruments or fragmentation methods) and biological aspects (such as sample types or disease types), the data currently collected in the atlas showed a high degree of diversity, thereby demonstrating the comprehensiveness of our atlas (
Supplementary Figure S2
).
By re-analyzing the whole atlas using the computational pipeline aforementioned, we identified a total of 2 028 964 unique peptides at a local peptide level FDR of 1%, which represent a 10.8-fold increase in comparison with the atlas v1.0. As MS-based immunopeptidomic datasets have been continuously generated and accumulated over the last ten years (Figure
2A
), our analysis showed a similarly continued increase of distinct peptides and binders identified, suggesting that saturation level might not be reached and the collection of the immunopeptidome remains incomplete (Figure
2B
and
C
). In total, it yielded 24 188 321 and 13 726 081 peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) for MHC class I immunopeptidome and class II immunopeptidome, respectively. These PSMs had a total of 1 000 585 and 1 123 828 unique peptide sequences for MHC class I immunopeptidome and class II immunopeptidome, respectively. Compared with the previous version of the atlas and other existing resources, the SysteMHC atlas v2.0 currently represents the largest collection of MHC immunopeptidomes (
Supplementary Figure S3
). Peptides were annotated as binders (or MHC-bound peptides) against a given MHC allotype if netMHCpan-4.1 or netMHCIIpan-4.0 reported percentile rank scores below 2.0 or 5.0, respectively (
36
). In total, we identified 457 360 MHC class I binders and 342 478 MHC class II binders. These binders can be attributed to 153 MHC class I allotypes and 149 MHC class II allotypes (Figure
2D
and
E
). Note that the fractions of peptides to be confidently predicted to be binders is <50%. It is mainly because the allele information of quite a few immunopeptidomics datasets was not provided by the original publication and we were not able to perform the analysis to predict the binders.

An important update of this atlas is to unravel various PTM types across the immunopeptidome. Applying the open search strategy enabled by MSFragger (
32
), our analysis identified 461 496 modified peptides, a 20.1-fold increase to that in v1.0. It took up 22.7% of the total pool of the immunopeptidome when the total number of unique peptides identified in the atlas was 2 028 964. Both unmodified and modified peptide showed their characteristic length distributions for both class I and class II immunopeptidomes (Figure
2F
). Currently, the atlas contains 61 distinct modification types (i.e. 422 distinct amino acid - PTM combinations) found on MHC-bound peptides. Not surprisingly, chemical modifications that are introduced during MS sample preparation are frequently observed, which can be exemplified by methionine oxidation (the only variable modification allowed in the closed search). Apart from chemical modifications, the atlas identified biological modifications that probably reflect the altered protein state in the cell, such as acetylation, glycosylation, methylation, phosphorylation, etc. (Figure
2G
and
H
). For instance, it was interesting to note a higher portion of glycosylation in MHC class II immunopeptidome relative to that in MHC class I immunopeptidome (
Supplementary Figure S4
), an independent validation of the finding reported in a recent study (
29
). This can be explained by the fact that N-glycans withstand MHC class II antigen processing and remain attached while N-linked glycans are removed prior to cytosolic degradation. For more statistics and information related to PTMs, refer to
Supplementary Figures S5–S7
, and the web portal for details.
The web portal
The SysteMHC Atlas 2.0 web portal at
https://systemhc.sjtu.edu.cn
provides four basic interfaces: Datasets, Explore, Statistics and Download, enabling large immunopeptidomic datasets and the whole repository to be explored in a user-specifiable fashion. The descriptions of each interface are as follows.
Datasets interface. The ‘Datasets’ interface allows users to investigate a specific sample or a dataset. This dataset can be found by searching ‘SYSMHC_ID’, ‘Project_name’ (publication title), ‘PubMed_ID’, ‘PRIDE_ID’ and ‘IEDB_ID’ (
45
). Users can select a dataset and then click on ‘View dataset’ at the bottom left to show all the samples related to this dataset (Figure
3A
). The displayed page then lists all the samples related, together with their metadata (Figure
3B
). Users can select one sample and click on the menus at the bottom to get specific results (Figure
3C
–
I
). The ‘PTM heatmap’ interface is newly added to show quantitative information of PTMs across various modification types and sites. The ‘MHC specific motifs’ interface is newly added to show the binding motifs. The FDR estimation module shown in Figure
3F
is newly added, which provides an option to check the results generated by different FDR estimation methods (i.e. global, separated and transferred FDR estimation)

). Users can use the ‘Non-UniProt peptides’ interface, which is newly added, to search for non-UniProt peptides that are not present in the UniProt protein database (Figure

). As described above, those peptides represent possible canonical mutated peptides and/or non-canonical peptides not found in UniProt. Each identified non-UniProt peptide is associated with Sample IDs, allele information, binding affinity scores, and the customized protein database linked to a downloadable fasta file, which was used in the original study.

46
) are provided for easy and external reference.

Spectral libraries
As an important data resource in analytical chemistry as well as one major component of the atlas, spectral libraries contain consensus spectra that are merged from replicative spectra generated from the same peptide ion. Obtained from multiple repetitive measurements across the repository, these consensus spectra are the most representative after stringent quality control and enjoy the best quality in terms of signal-to-noise ratio. Indeed, thanks to its sensitivity and considerate search space, spectral libraries have already been applied to a few data dependent acquisition (DDA) MS-based immunopeptidomics studies, demonstrating its utility and improved sensitivity in MHC-bound peptide identifications (
47
,
48
). Recently, data independent acquisition (DIA)-MS immunopeptidomic analysis has become increasingly popular, due to its greater sensitivity, higher reproducibility and better quantitative accuracy. As prior knowledge or sometimes a prerequisite for DIA-MS analysis, the availability of spectral library and its comprehensiveness are undoubtedly essential to perform immunopeptidomic analysis quantitatively and qualitatively.
In the current release of the atlas, 2447 context-specific, 303 allele-specific and 122 PTM-specific high-quality spectral libraries were carefully curated and built from 6.3 TB complex mass spectrometric data. The libraries can be further split according to their fragmentation methods (e.g. HCD; CID; ETD and ‘QTOF’ for HCD in QTOF MS). These libraries are compatible with the format released by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and can be directly applied to both DDA and DIA analysis, supporting popular DIA workflows such as DIA-NN and Spectronaut (
49–51
). Further, being high-quality and comprehensive, spectral libraries can be used as training data for computational algorithms, such as MS spectra prediction, retention time prediction and binding affinity estimation, which can in return accelerate the next generation of AI-based algorithms for immunopeptidomic analysis. Last, as resources are collected across the whole repository, the spectral library is comprehensive and data mining in spectral libraries may lead to the extraction of useful biological insights (
50
) or the finding of possible bias introduced from technical aspects (
52
). For example, through simple data mining in the spectral library, we confirmed that in the atlas, cysteines were consistently under-represented in immunopeptidomic analyses (
Supplementary Figure S8
). This has also been reported in several studies, which can be explained by the fact that chemical modifications on cysteines can likely occur during the immunopeptidomic experimental workflow (
11
,
53
,
54
). We also noticed the depletion of methionine and tryptophan, which accords with the finding in (
55
). These findings may help to call the attention of specific developments to avoid such technical bias, thereby enabling a more comprehensive capture and presentation of antigen processing.
Conclusion
Data sharing, reproducible data analysis and community repository resources become increasingly necessary and valuable in life sciences, especially when huge amounts of data have been generated. Along this line, the datasets and functions of the SysteMHC atlas v2.0 have been significantly improved. First, the scope of the atlas is expanded to over 7000 MS raw files obtained from 2447 biological samples across five species. With increased immunopeptidome coverage on various alleles, a total number of 1.0 million and 1.1 million unique peptides were identified for MHC class I and class II immunopeptidome, respectively. Second, to identify MHC-bound peptides carrying on unexpected PTMs in an unbiased manner, we developed an integrative pipeline that allows one-stop reproducible analysis for immunopeptidomic datasets. Third, various comprehensive and high-quality spectral libraries are provided as community resources for data mining, algorithm development and future usage in immunopeptidomic and proteomic analysis.
Due to its important clinical implications in precision medicine, immunopeptidomics is an emerging research field that is expanding rapidly, and we expect that the number of immunopeptidomic datasets will grow substantially in the near future. In addition, the recent fast development of deep learning-based tools to predict tandem spectra and retention time as well as re-scoring algorithms associated boosts the identification of immunopeptidome (
48
,
56–58
). Along this line, we will continue collecting new datasets, adding new tools and functions, and generating associated analysis results to upgrade the atlas periodically, which will improve our understanding of immunology and eventually pave the way to the development of cancer immunotherapies.
